name: Epicurean friendship and its tension with egoistic hedonism
plain_explanation: Epicurus taught that everyone always acts only for their own pleasure, yet he also prized friendship enormously and clearly loved his friends and their children without any calculating self-interest -- a tension Russell says Epicurus himself did not fully resolve.
precise_definition: Epicurus regarded friendship as the safest of social pleasures and, per Cicero, held it must be cultivated because life without it is neither safe, fearless, nor pleasant; yet he also stated that 'all friendship is desirable in itself,' a claim in tension with his official theory that all human action is ultimately self-interested pleasure-seeking.
why_it_mattered: Illustrates, for Russell, a recurring pattern in ethical egoists (he draws the same comparison for Bentham): personal warmth and generosity that exceed what their own theory of human motivation would strictly predict or require.
historical_origin: Reflected throughout Epicurus's surviving letters, which show real affection for his community ('our holy body') and for the children of his deceased friend Metrodorus, whom he provided for in his will.
examples: Epicurus's dying letter asking his correspondent to look after Metrodorus's children
His warm, informal letters to children of community members
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell draws a direct parallel to Jeremy Bentham, 'constantly seduced by his own kindly and affectionate nature into admirable behaviour' beyond what his official hedonist theory required.
